mods.abstract: On March 18, 2011, the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco and the B.E. Journal of Macroeconomics (BEJM) hosted a conference exploring the use of geographical data in empirical macroeconomics. The papers presented used geographically disaggregated data to explore a range of macroeconomic issues, including wealth effects on consumption, the effectiveness of fiscal and monetary policies, and the impact of banking regulations. The conference featured remarks from Hal Varian, Chief Economist of Google, who discussed the use of internet query and shopping data in the construction of real-time economic indicators, along with some geographical applications.

mods.note: ﻿"The Consular Reports series was first issued in 1880 as monthly documents numbered consecutively. A few months were missed in the publication run, and in some months a second issue appeared and was given a "half" number (e.g., 24 1/2). Occasionally an issue appeared with a special title, but after 1890 these special reports were published as Special Consular Reports (S 4.9:). The Consular Reports were published originally by the State Department's Bureau of Statistics (later known as the Bureau of Foreign Commerce), but in 1903 the agency was transferred to the new Department of Commerce and Labor as the Bureau of Statistics. It then moved to the Manufactures Bureau in 1905 under the title Monthly Consular and Trade Reports, where it was published until June 1910." -- U.S. Congressional Serial Set Finding List: Consular Reports (S 4.7:, C 14.8:, C 10.6:)﻿

﻿State Department, Bureau of Statistics/Foreign Commerce, No 1 (1855)-No. 277 (June 1903); Department of Commerce and Labor, Bureau of Statistics, No. 278 (Nov. 1903)-no. 297 (June 1905); Department of Commerce and Labor, Bureau of Manufactures, No. 298 (July 1905)-no. 357 (June 1910).﻿
